newsitem.title: ITALY: Dutch-Flemish show goes to roots of modern art.
newsitem.headline: Dutch-Flemish show goes to roots of modern art.

text.p: It is famously easy to get lost in Venice and visitors to one of the elegant palazzos on the Grand Canal might well wonder where they went wrong when they turn up to see a new show on Dutch and Flemish modern art.
The first thing they see is a life-sized black figure with a board proclaiming: "I have nothing to do with the 20th century".
The second is a painting from 1531.
The show at the Palazzo Grassi brings together late 19th and early 20th century art from Flanders and the Netherlands for the first time, tracing its influences back through the ages.
"We want people to look at art afresh and not through cliches," said Jan Hoet, director of the Museum van Hedendaagse Kunst in the Belgian city of Ghent and co-curator of the exhibition.
"We wanted to expose the deep roots...to show the linearity and the divisions," he said.

The exhibition, which traces the development of modern art in the Low Countries from artists such as Vincent Van Gogh, James Ensor, Rene Magritte and Piet Mondrian to contemporary artists, is not just concerned with history. It is also about geography.
Rudi Fuchs, director of Amsterdam's Stedelijk Museum, said the it highlighted how modern Dutch and Flemish artists had reacted differently to the trends of their times.

"For example, Picasso and Braque invented cubism," Fuchs said, referring to the Spanish and French artists whose radical rejection of a flat view of reality in favour of angular visions to show an object from all sides gave birth to abstract art.
"With Mondrian, in his own Dutch orbit, Cubism intersected with his love for 17th century landscapes, harmony and stillness and led to paintings of extreme silence," Fuchs said.
Mondrian is best known for bold, bright geometric grids.

"In Belgium, Gustave de Smet also saw cubism but he developed its chiaroscuro (the play of light and dark) aspect...It's about what you do with the ingredients. The ultimate conclusion is that modern art is a set of versions."
COMPARE AND CONTRAST -- VAN GOGH AND ENSOR
The exhibition took more than two years to organise and contains 220 works by 89 artists. Despite its cliche-busting aims, Fuchs said some cultural stereotypes had turned out to be true.
Hoet said the Flemish tended to lose themselves in their imagination while the Dutch were often quieter and, in the case of Van Gogh, more concerned with the search for truth.
Van Gogh's work is one of the starting points of the show, where viewers are invited to compare and contrast his style with that of Ensor, a Belgian who was seven years his junior.
Some familiar works by Van Gogh are on display, including a self-portrait from 1887 and a landscape with cedar trees from 1890. Lesser-known works were also picked as a challenge.
While Ensor ranged from sober scenes to atmospheric seascapes and bright, sometimes burlesque works, and declared: "I intend to ignore my influences", Van Gogh focused on nature.
But Van Gogh concluded that trying to capture "character" meant his representations were sometimes stranger than reality.
The curators said that putting the two artists together like this for the first time in an exhibition was key to their aim of encouraging people to look at familiar artists with new eyes.
"I had never really realised how much they have in common," said Dutch junior culture minister Aad Nuis after his tour.
CROSS-REFERENCES -- ART AS LIVING HISTORY

Echoes abound as the show unfolds through symbolism, expressionism, abstraction, surrealism and varied trends since World War Two in an 18th century palazzo in the famous Italian lagoon city that, like the Netherlands, is built on water.

The most striking parallel between old and new comes near the end of the show, where the legacy of the 17th century Dutch painter Pieter Saenredam is linked to Mondrian's work in the 1920s and contemporary artist Jan Dibbets.
Saenredam, in a painting from 1661, plays with perspective by showing a series of doors opening onto courtyards.
"Saenredam's churches were an eye-opener to me," says, Dibbets, a Dutchman. "They made me realise that he was actually a 17th century Mondrian."
Dibbets's own work -- huge monochrome backgrounds with photographs of windows in the centre that twist perspectives -- themselves recall the lines and angles of Mondrian.
One of Dibbets's works, in which a square window is viewed at an angle and appears diamond shaped, also recalls the floating windows of Belgian surrealist Rene Magritte.
One of Magritte's works in the exhibition, showing a green rhinoceros climbing a blue-and-white column against a red background, has never been seen outside Belgium, Hoet said.
Jeroen Henneman, a Dutch artist whose work is on show, said the "amazing, beautiful" exhibition was full of insights.

"Now I'm able to look at works from 40 years ago and put them in the same historical context as Titian in his time," he said, referring to the great 16th century Venetian artist considered one of the founding fathers of modern painting.
"There's less difference than there's supposed to be."
The exhibition, called Flemish and Dutch Painting, runs at the Palazzo Grassi until July 13.
